screens.title: Introduction to Software Engineering and the SDLC
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson you will meet software engineering as a disciplined practice for building reliable systems, and you will learn the common stages of the Software Development Life Cycle. Software engineering treats software like a long-lived engineered product: it needs planning, design, verification, deployment, and maintenance. That perspective reduces surprises, keeps costs predictable, and improves quality over the long run. You will also compare two common ways to organize work: the sequential Waterfall approach and iterative cycles that let teams learn and adapt. A concrete example you will revisit is choosing an approach for an embedded flight control system versus a fast-changing mobile feature. For safety-critical, tightly specified systems the sequential approach can be appropriate because requirements are stable. For user-facing apps that change quickly, iterative development helps you get feedback early and reduce risk. As you move through the chapter, notice common pitfalls like skipping requirements or shortening test cycles, and learn simple mitigations such as early stakeholder feedback and continuous testing. By the end you should be able to pick an SDLC approach and explain why it fits a given project.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Introduction
Introduction to Software Engineering and the SDLC
A structured approach to building, delivering, and maintaining reliable software.
Orientation

Software engineering applies disciplined methods to software development so teams can deliver predictable, maintainable solutions. You will learn common SDLC phases, why each matters, and how to select between Waterfall and Iterative approaches depending on project risk and change.

In this lesson
Define software engineering and SDLC phases
Coming up
Compare Waterfall and Iterative models
Outcome
Choose an SDLC for a scenario and justify it
Concept map
How phases connect from idea to maintenance
Requirements
Define goals and user needs.
Design
Plan architecture and interfaces.
Implementation
Write and assemble code.
Testing
Verify behavior and quality.
Deployment
Make software available to users.
Maintenance
Update, fix, and improve over time.
Quick takeaway
Software engineering organizes work so teams can build dependable products and manage change across a system's lifetime.

screens.title: What is Software Engineering?
screens.narratorSegment: Software engineering is a systematic, disciplined, and quantifiable approach to the development, operation, and maintenance of software. That definition means we treat software as an engineered product that needs planning, specification, verification, and maintenance. A concrete example is preparing a full requirements document and design before writing code for an embedded system: teams create detailed specifications, review them, and verify compliance because the cost of failure is high. A common misconception is that software engineering is just writing code better. In reality it includes processes around requirements, design decisions, testing strategies, documentation, and maintenance plans. Another contrast is between ad-hoc scripting for a one-off task and engineering a system intended to run and be supported for years: the latter demands traceability, quality controls, and measurable practices. Key elements you should remember are reproducible processes, measurable outcomes, and a focus on maintainability. Try to think of software engineering as the discipline that lets teams deliver predictable results: it does not remove uncertainty but reduces it through structure and measurement. What practice from your experience would you adopt to make a small project more engineering-led?

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › What is Software Engineering?
Definition

Software engineering is a systematic, disciplined, and quantifiable approach to developing, operating, and maintaining software. It goes beyond coding to include planning, quality assurance, documentation, and maintainability.

Metaphor: treat software like a building with blueprints and inspection.
Common misconception

Software engineering is not just writing cleaner code; it includes processes, artifacts, and planning that support long-term reliability.

Concrete example

For an embedded flight control system, teams create detailed requirements and verification plans before coding. This ensures compliance with safety rules and lowers the chance of catastrophic failures.

Key Takeaway

Engineering practices make complex software predictable and maintainable across its lifecycle.

screens.title: SDLC Overview: Phases and Flow
screens.narratorSegment: The Software Development Life Cycle is a framework that outlines major phases from idea to long-term support. The typical phases are requirements gathering, design, implementation or coding, testing, deployment, and maintenance. Requirements gathering clarifies what the system must do and who it serves. Design turns requirements into architecture, components, and interfaces. Implementation writes the software according to the design. Testing verifies the system meets requirements and reveals defects. Deployment makes the software available to users, and maintenance handles updates, fixes, and enhancements. A simple example is building a web feature: start by listing user stories, then design the UI and A P I, implement the code, run unit and integration tests, deploy to production, and later fix bugs or add new capabilities. One common confusion is thinking testing only happens after implementation; in practice testing planning begins early, and some tests are automated continuously. Another misconception is treating maintenance as an afterthought — in reality it is a long phase that often consumes more effort than the original build. Key takeaway: map each artifact you produce (requirements doc, diagrams, test plan, deployment checklist) to its SDLC phase so you can track progress and manage risk.

keyIdea.title: Phase map
keyIdea.text: Each SDLC phase produces artifacts and reduces uncertainty; early testing planning and maintenance planning are essential.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › SDLC Overview
SDLC Timeline
Requirements
Identify goals, users, and constraints; produce a requirements document or user stories.
Design
Plan architecture, components, and interfaces.
Implementation
Write code, integrate components, and prepare builds.
Testing
Plan and run tests to validate requirements and quality.
Deployment
Release software to users using deployment checklists or pipelines.
Maintenance
Fix bugs, patch vulnerabilities, and evolve functionality over time.
Explanation and example

Consider a new web feature: write user stories in requirements, design the UI and API, implement components, create unit and integration tests, deploy via a pipeline, then monitor and maintain. Plan tests and maintenance early so they are part of the process rather than afterthoughts.

Common mistake
Delaying test planning until after implementation leads to missed defects and higher cost to fix them.
Key takeaway
Map artifacts to phases and schedule testing and maintenance from day one.

screens.title: Requirements Gathering
screens.narratorSegment: Requirements gathering is the phase where you discover what the system must do and why. Good requirements identify user needs, business constraints, and nonfunctional expectations such as performance or safety. A concrete example is writing user stories for a login feature: the story should state who the user is, what they want to do, and why it matters. Requirements should be testable and traceable so you can verify implementation later. A frequent mistake is treating requirements as optional or high-level notes rather than formal artifacts; this leads to building the wrong feature. To avoid that, use simple strategies: involve stakeholders early, write acceptance criteria, and keep a traceability matrix linking requirements to tests and design elements. Another pitfall is assuming requirements will never change; instead plan for change by prioritizing and breaking large requirements into smaller deliverable slices. Key takeaway: invest time in clear, testable requirements so downstream phases run smoothly and rework is minimized. Requirements Gathering means clear, testable, and traceable requirements reduce rework and ensure the team builds the right product.. In practical terms, capture goals, users, and constraints precisely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Requirements Gathering
Definition and goal

Collect user needs, constraints, and success criteria. Produce artifacts like user stories, acceptance criteria, or a requirements document so later work can be validated against them.

Mnemonic: write acceptance criteria for each requirement.
Common mistake

Skipping formal requirements leads to building features that miss user needs.

Example: login user story
As a registered user, I want to sign in using my email and password so I can access personalized content. Acceptance criteria: valid credentials succeed, invalid credentials show an error, and all attempts are logged.
Key Takeaway

Make requirements testable and traceable; involve stakeholders early and write acceptance criteria.

screens.title: Design Phase
screens.narratorSegment: Design transforms requirements into a plan for how the system will be built. It captures architecture, component boundaries, interfaces, data structures, and nonfunctional considerations like performance and security. A concrete example is choosing an architecture for a login system: decide whether authentication is centralized, how the A P I will communicate with the UI, and how credentials are stored securely. A common misconception is that design always means long, formal diagrams; in many teams design can be lightweight sketches and component contracts that are sufficient for implementation. The key is to document decisions that affect later work and to include security and testing concerns in the design. Another important point is that good design helps divide work among teams and establishes clear integration points, reducing surprises during implementation. Key takeaway: capture the essential architectural decisions and interfaces so implementation and testing align with the intended behavior. Design Phase means design declares architecture and interfaces so teams can implement components that integrate cleanly and meet nonfunctional goals.. In practical terms, plan architecture, components, and interfaces. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Design Phase
What design captures
  • Architecture and component boundaries
  • Interfaces and data contracts
  • Nonfunctional requirements like performance and security
Misconception

Design isn't always heavyweight documentation; pragmatic diagrams and interface contracts often suffice if decisions are recorded.

Concrete example

For a login subsystem decide where authentication runs, how tokens are issued, how the UI talks to the API, and how credentials are secured and audited.

Key Takeaway

Document key decisions and interfaces so implementation and testing teams have a clear contract to build against.

screens.title: Implementation (Coding)
screens.narratorSegment: Implementation is where the team writes code and assembles components according to design. Good implementation follows agreed standards, uses version control, and keeps changes small and reviewable. A concrete scenario from this chapter is implementing a core login in an early iteration: deliver a minimal working login, add automated tests, and keep commits focused on a single behavior. One misconception is that faster coding equals faster delivery; in fact, bypassing code review, skipping tests, or ignoring coding standards typically increases later cost and defects. To reduce risk, use small pull requests, automated tests, and continuous integration. Below you will find a short pseudocode example showing how an iteration might add authentication then later add profile management. This example demonstrates incremental delivery: start with a minimal end-to-end path and expand features in later cycles. Key takeaway: implement small, testable increments and automate builds to catch integration issues early. Implementation (Coding) means write code in small, reviewed increments with automated tests and ci to reduce integration risk.. In practical terms, turn design into working software with clear practices. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Implementation
Implementation practices
  • Use version control and small, focused commits.
  • Automate tests and integrate continuous builds.
  • Enforce code review and coding standards.
Concrete incremental example
<-- iteration 1: minimal login -->
function login(userCredentials) {
  // validate input
  // check credentials against store
  // return session token on success
}

<-- iteration 2: add user profile -->
function getUserProfile(userId) {
  // fetch profile data
  // return profile fields
}
Note: pseudocode illustrates delivering a working login first, then adding profile functionality in a later iteration.
Key Takeaway

Keep changes small and testable. Deliver a minimal working path, then add features iteratively to reduce integration surprises.

screens.title: Testing Phase
screens.narratorSegment: Testing is the disciplined activity of evaluating software to find defects and confirm requirements are met. It includes unit tests, integration tests, system tests, and acceptance tests. A concrete example is writing unit tests for the login function to verify valid and invalid credentials behave as expected, and integration tests that confirm the login token works with other services. A common misconception is relying only on manual testing or assuming that no reported bugs means the system is ready. Automated tests catch regressions and make repeated verification affordable. Another issue is deferring tests until late in the project; when testing starts late, defects discovered can force costly rework. A better approach is to plan tests during requirements and run them continuously during implementation using automated pipelines. Key takeaway: invest in a layered testing strategy and automate where possible so defects are discovered quickly and costs to fix remain low. Testing Phase means plan and automate tests early to detect defects quickly and keep fix costs low.. In practical terms, verify the system meets requirements and find defects early. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Testing Phase
Test types
  • Unit tests validate individual functions or modules.
  • Integration tests validate interactions between components.
  • Acceptance tests confirm requirements are met from a user perspective.
Example: login testing

Write unit tests for credential validation, integration tests for token exchange, and acceptance tests to ensure the login flow works end-to-end.

Common mistake
Starting testing late or relying only on manual tests increases the chance of late defects and expensive fixes.
Key Takeaway
Automate layered tests and run them continuously so defects are caught early and reliably.

screens.title: Deployment
screens.narratorSegment: Deployment is the process that delivers software to users in a controlled and repeatable way. It often uses pipelines or checklists to ensure builds, configuration, and validation steps complete successfully before release. A practical example is deploying a web feature through a pipeline that builds, runs tests, deploys to staging, runs smoke tests, then promotes to production. A common misconception is that deployment is a single final step; instead it is an operational workflow that should be automated, monitored, and reversible when necessary. Another issue is insufficient deployment validation: without smoke tests or health checks, problems can reach users. To mitigate risk, use automated pipelines, staged environments, and deployment rollback strategies. Key takeaway: design deployment as a repeatable, observable process so releases are predictable and recoverable when issues occur. Deployment means automated pipelines, staged releases, and validation checks make production releases predictable and safer.. In practical terms, move software into production with repeatable steps. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Deployment
Deployment pipeline steps
  1. Build and package the release.
  2. Run automated tests and static checks.
  3. Deploy to staging and run smoke tests.
  4. Promote to production and monitor health.
Example: staged release

A staged release deploys to a small subset of users or a staging environment first, observes behavior, then gradually increases exposure if results are healthy.

Remember to include rollback procedures and monitoring for quick recovery.
Key Takeaway

Treat deployment as an automated, observable process with staged validation and rollback options to reduce user impact from failures.

screens.title: Maintenance and Security Integration
screens.narratorSegment: Maintenance is the ongoing activity of fixing defects, applying updates, and evolving the system after deployment. It often consumes more effort over time than the initial build. Integrating security throughout the SDLC means including secure design principles in the design phase, using secure coding practices during implementation, and performing security testing as part of your test suite. A concrete example is adding threat modeling during design and static security scans during implementation to catch vulnerabilities before they reach production. A common misconception is to treat security as a separate final check; this approach lets vulnerabilities slip in and increases remediation cost. Instead, make security a recurring task across requirements, design, implementation, testing, and maintenance. Another risk in maintenance is poor documentation: without clear documentation, later teams spend extra time discovering intent and behavior. Key takeaway: plan for maintenance and embed security tasks in each SDLC phase so the system remains robust and protected over time. screens.title: Waterfall vs Iterative Models
screens.narratorSegment: Two common SDLC models illustrate different trade-offs. The Waterfall model is sequential: each phase completes before the next begins. It works well when requirements are stable, such as for highly regulated or safety-critical embedded systems. Its strength is clarity and documented checkpoints, but its weakness is rigidity: changes discovered late are costly. The Iterative model splits work into repeated cycles, delivering a basic system that evolves through successive iterations. Iterative development enables early feedback, reduces risk by revealing issues sooner, and is a better fit for rapidly changing requirements, such as a new social media feature. A common misconception is that iterative means no planning; in fact each iteration still includes requirements, design, implementation, and testing on a smaller scale. A practical comparison: for a flight control system choose Waterfall because requirements are fixed and verification is rigorous; for a live video social feature choose Iterative to gather early user feedback and adjust quickly. Key takeaway: match the model to project needs—stability and regulatory constraints favor Waterfall, evolving requirements favor Iterative. fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this lesson you will meet software engineering as a disciplined practice for building reliable systems, and you will learn the common stages of the Software Development Life Cycle. Software engineering treats software like a long-lived engineered product: it needs planning, design, verification, deployment, and maintenance. That perspective reduces surprises, keeps costs predictable, and improves quality over the long run. You will also compare two common ways to organize work: the sequential Waterfall approach and iterative cycles that let teams learn and adapt. A concrete example you will revisit is choosing an approach for an embedded flight control system versus a fast-changing mobile feature. For safety-critical, tightly specified systems the sequential approach can be appropriate because requirements are stable. For user-facing apps that change quickly, iterative development helps you get feedback early and reduce risk. As you move through the chapter, notice common pitfalls like skipping requirements or shortening test cycles, and learn simple mitigations such as early stakeholder feedback and continuous testing. By the end you should be able to pick an SDLC approach and explain why it fits a given project.

In this section we list precise learning goals so you can measure your progress. First, you will be able to define software engineering in terms of a disciplined, measurable practice for developing and maintaining software. That definition matters because it frames decisions about quality, process, and long-term support. Second, you will describe the typical phases of the Software Development Life Cycle: requirements, design, implementation, testing, deployment, and maintenance. Understanding these phases helps you identify where risks are highest and where to apply practices like testing and documentation. Each objective below includes a short explanation and a simple visual cue to help you remember the skill. As you study each lesson, match your understanding to these objectives and use the verified competency milestone as a target for practice tasks and assessments.

This continuation clarifies how you will demonstrate each objective through practice. For defining software engineering, you will produce a short written definition and contrast it with ad-hoc coding practices. This shows you can explain why discipline matters in project planning. For SDLC phases, you will map a small project to each phase and note typical deliverables, such as a requirements document, design diagrams, test plans, and deployment checklists. For comparing SDLC models, you'll choose a model for two scenarios and justify your selection. This task requires reasoning about stability of requirements, safety-critical constraints, and expected change. For pitfalls and mitigations, you will list common mistakes and a short mitigation plan that includes at least one testing or security strategy. These competency activities are intentionally practical: they mirror real decisions teams make and will prepare you to discuss trade-offs clearly with stakeholders.

Software engineering is a systematic, disciplined, and quantifiable approach to the development, operation, and maintenance of software. That definition means we treat software as an engineered product that needs planning, specification, verification, and maintenance. A concrete example is preparing a full requirements document and design before writing code for an embedded system: teams create detailed specifications, review them, and verify compliance because the cost of failure is high. A common misconception is that software engineering is just writing code better. In reality it includes processes around requirements, design decisions, testing strategies, documentation, and maintenance plans. Another contrast is between ad-hoc scripting for a one-off task and engineering a system intended to run and be supported for years: the latter demands traceability, quality controls, and measurable practices. Key elements you should remember are reproducible processes, measurable outcomes, and a focus on maintainability. Try to think of software engineering as the discipline that lets teams deliver predictable results: it does not remove uncertainty but reduces it through structure and measurement. What practice from your experience would you adopt to make a small project more engineering-led?

The Software Development Life Cycle is a framework that outlines major phases from idea to long-term support. The typical phases are requirements gathering, design, implementation or coding, testing, deployment, and maintenance. Requirements gathering clarifies what the system must do and who it serves. Design turns requirements into architecture, components, and interfaces. Implementation writes the software according to the design. Testing verifies the system meets requirements and reveals defects. Deployment makes the software available to users, and maintenance handles updates, fixes, and enhancements. A simple example is building a web feature: start by listing user stories, then design the UI and A P I, implement the code, run unit and integration tests, deploy to production, and later fix bugs or add new capabilities. One common confusion is thinking testing only happens after implementation; in practice testing planning begins early, and some tests are automated continuously. Another misconception is treating maintenance as an afterthought — in reality it is a long phase that often consumes more effort than the original build. Key takeaway: map each artifact you produce (requirements doc, diagrams, test plan, deployment checklist) to its SDLC phase so you can track progress and manage risk.

Requirements gathering is the phase where you discover what the system must do and why. Good requirements identify user needs, business constraints, and nonfunctional expectations such as performance or safety. A concrete example is writing user stories for a login feature: the story should state who the user is, what they want to do, and why it matters. Requirements should be testable and traceable so you can verify implementation later. A frequent mistake is treating requirements as optional or high-level notes rather than formal artifacts; this leads to building the wrong feature. To avoid that, use simple strategies: involve stakeholders early, write acceptance criteria, and keep a traceability matrix linking requirements to tests and design elements. Another pitfall is assuming requirements will never change; instead plan for change by prioritizing and breaking large requirements into smaller deliverable slices. Key takeaway: invest time in clear, testable requirements so downstream phases run smoothly and rework is minimized. Design transforms requirements into a plan for how the system will be built. It captures architecture, component boundaries, interfaces, data structures, and nonfunctional considerations like performance and security. A concrete example is choosing an architecture for a login system: decide whether authentication is centralized, how the A P I will communicate with the UI, and how credentials are stored securely. A common misconception is that design always means long, formal diagrams; in many teams design can be lightweight sketches and component contracts that are sufficient for implementation. The key is to document decisions that affect later work and to include security and testing concerns in the design. Another important point is that good design helps divide work among teams and establishes clear integration points, reducing surprises during implementation. Testing is the disciplined activity of evaluating software to find defects and confirm requirements are met. It includes unit tests, integration tests, system tests, and acceptance tests. To mitigate risk, use automated pipelines, staged environments, and deployment rollback strategies.
